heading: The Legal / Ethical Grid
title: Real instances placed on the legal/ethical grid
rows: Paying 'chiya kharcha' to push your file up the pile
Sharing one paid Netflix/Canva login among 8 friends
Using 'source-force' to skip a government-office queue
Selling legally-collected customer data without consent
Paying your taxes honestly and on time
Whistle-blowing on employer fraud, breaking an NDA
A student pirating software they cannot afford
Leaking a customer's private photos from a database
note: The danger zone is legal-but-unethical: nothing external stops you there — only your own judgment. Most everyday harm lives in that quadrant.

heading: Ethics in the Business World
title: Profit vs trust — real Nepali business choices
rows: Festival shop triples oil/sugar price in a Dashain shortage
Customers desert it every Dashain after
Trekking agency hides a route safety risk to keep a booking
Client harmed; lawsuits; scares off future tourists
A wallet (eSewa/Khalti-style) quietly reuses data for ads
Users switch wallets once they find out
A Daraz seller ships a counterfeit as genuine
A bank buries fees in the fine print
A college promises placements it cannot deliver
A momo restaurant reuses stale ingredients to cut cost
note: Trust is slow to build and instant to lose — each shortcut spends a years-long reserve. Good ethics is usually good business on a longer clock.

heading: Why Good People & Businesses Still Go Wrong
title: Ordinary people, predictable pressure — name the cause
rows: Junior accountant rounds up numbers because 'everyone here does'
Sales rep oversells a policy to hit target or lose the job
Clerk approves a shortcut because 'no one audits this desk'
Staffer follows a manager's 'just do it' on a dodgy file
IT admin skips a security patch because the team never bothers
Bank teller waives KYC for a VIP under branch-target pressure
Team member stays silent though the plan clearly feels wrong
note: No villains here — the failures are situational. Change the conditions (leadership, oversight, consequences) and the behaviour changes. Fix the situation, not just the person.

heading: Carroll's CSR Pyramid
title: Real Nepali activities sorted onto Carroll's four levels
rows: A commercial bank staying solvent and profitable
A bank allocating a share of profit to CSR as NRB directs
A firm paying all taxes and following labour law
A company paying fair wages and advertising honestly
Right beyond what the law forces
A telecom NOT exploiting a billing loophole that overcharges
Ncell/NTC extending coverage to remote villages
A bank funding scholarships and flood relief
note: A company donating to charity (top) while underpaying staff (skipping the ethical layer) is doing CSR backwards — image without foundation.

heading: Stakeholder Theory
title: One decision, two lenses — real Nepali cases
rows: A brick/cement factory profitable but polluting a village's water
A wallet firm sells user location data to advertisers
A garment exporter underpays workers to win a contract
A bank pushes loans farmers can't repay
A college over-enrols far beyond capacity
A hydropower project skips community consultation
note: The costs pushed onto non-owner stakeholders are hidden, not absent — they return as lawsuits, boycotts, or a lost social licence to operate.

heading: Fostering CSR & an Ethical Culture
title: Genuine CSR or greenwashing? Apply the test
rows: Bank ad 'we care about farmers' while loan terms crush them
A firm plants trees for a photo op but pollutes a river daily
'Eco-friendly' labels added with no change to the packaging
A one-off Dashain donation heavily used in ads by a low-wage employer
A firm with years of fair wages runs a modest 'we treat staff well' campaign
Telecom runs real rural-coverage & digital-literacy programs
A bank publishes an audited social-responsibility report matching practice
note: The ad is never the evidence — the operation is. One-line test: does the company's everyday behaviour match its CSR message?

heading: From Values to Behaviour
title: Same code, opposite lessons — what staff actually learn
rows: A manager who takes a kickback is dismissed
The rules are real — follow them
A whistle-blower is thanked and protected
A reporter is sidelined and punished
Staff who peek at accounts are disciplined
A rushed, unsafe release is rolled back
Corners cut to ship on time, and praised
The code doesn't apply under pressure
note: The document is never the cause. An unenforced code is worse than none — it teaches everyone that the rules are for show.

heading: Measuring & Sustaining Ethics
title: How a violation is handled — and what everyone learns
rows: A senior and a junior both take a kickback
Senior excused, junior fired for the same breach
A culture survey flags a bullying manager
Reported concerns are collected but never acted on
An ethics audit finds a compliance gap
Fixed before it became a scandal
A branch skips the mandated AML training
A director's conflict of interest is disclosed
Ethics applies at the top too
note: Consistency is make-or-break. Selective punishment — excusing seniors — destroys trust faster than having no code at all, because the hypocrisy is visible.

heading: The 5-Step Decision Process
title: The process on six everyday dilemmas
rows: Classmate shares a Drive with tomorrow's exam answers
Are these really the exam? How did I get them?
A vendor offers your procurement officer a 'gift' before a tender
Gift or bribe? What's the policy limit?
Boss asks you to backdate an invoice
Is this legal? Why is it needed?
A user's data was leaked from your app
Friend asks you to share paid software licence keys
You spot a bug that overcharges some customers
How many affected, and by how much?
note: Steps 1-2 (get the facts, name the stakeholders) are the most-skipped and most important — that is where most bad decisions are born.

heading: Four Ethical Lenses
title: Which lens fits — and what it decides
rows: Ambulance asks to jump the fuel queue in a shortage
Lay off 10 staff to save 200 jobs
Greatest good for the greatest number
Read a subordinate's private chats 'for the company'
Pay two equally-qualified interns the same
Report a friend who is stealing from the till
What a person of good character does
Promote strictly on merit, not on 'source-force'
Use user data in a profitable way most would object to
Lenses disagree — name it, decide on merits
note: On easy cases the four lenses converge (which is why it feels obvious). The hard cases are exactly where they disagree — naming the disagreement is half the work.

heading: Common Decision Traps
title: How the traps sound in real life — and the counter
headers: What you hear in real life
rows: 'Everyone in this office rounds the numbers'
Name the act — would you defend it openly?
'The whole team agreed, so it must be fine'
Ask for one dissenting view; decide on merits
'Just fudge this one report, only this once'
Set the bright line before the pressure
'The manager told me to, so it's on him'
You remain responsible; run the 5 steps
'It's not really piracy — students do it all the time'
'Nobody will notice one skipped KYC check'
One exception lowers the bar for next time
'Don't rock the boat, the seniors already decided'
note: 'Just fudge this one report' uses two traps at once — blind obedience plus slippery slope. Naming the trap out loud strips half its power.

heading: Why IT Raises Distinct Ethical Challenges
title: Real IT incidents — the factor that makes each worse
rows: Personal data leaked from a Nepali online service
It can never be fully recalled
A default privacy setting exposes millions of accounts
One choice harms a whole population
A viral election deepfake the night before voting
An anonymous account harasses a victim across borders
Hard to catch or hold accountable
A loan algorithm rejects an entire neighbourhood
A leaked private photo re-shared across many groups
A new AI tool with no law yet governing its use
'Is it legal?' has no answer yet
note: Because the legal 'floor' is often missing in IT, your own ethics is frequently the only thing holding — this is where 'law is only the floor' matters most.

heading: The Four Pillars — 'PAPA'
title: Name the pillar — real IT / Nepal concerns
rows: An app sells your location data to advertisers
Who can collect and see your data
A wallet reuses your transaction history without consent
Data used beyond what you agreed to
A biased loan algorithm wrongly rejects you
Responsibility when the algorithm is wrong
Wrong info on a government portal blocks your service
Pirating Windows/Adobe or copying a code repo
Villages with no internet miss e-services (Nagarik App)
Who is left out — the digital divide
Only smartphone owners can use a digital-ID system
note: Security threads through all four pillars (Units 5-8). PAPA lets you name any IT-ethics concern precisely.

heading: The IT Professional's Responsibility
title: 'Can' vs 'Should' — you can, but should you?
rows: Scrape 100,000 users' public posts for a project
Public is not consent to THIS use
Log every keystroke of staff 'for productivity'
Sell 'anonymised' data that can be re-identified
Build a face-recognition tool from public photos
People didn't consent to be identified
Read user DMs because you have admin access
A/B test a dark pattern that tricks users into paying
Deploy an untested medical-advice chatbot because it 'works'
note: Professional codes (ACM, IEEE) exist to keep 'should' in front of 'can' — your duty is to the people in the data, not just to what is technically allowed.
